title: THEY USED THE NAME OF JESUS—AND THE DEMON ASKED, “WHO ARE YOU?”
paragraphs: THEY USED THE NAME OF JESUS—AND THE DEMON ASKED, “WHO ARE YOU?”

Seven religious men discovered something terrifying in Ephesus: you can have the name of Jesus on your lips without having surrendered your life to Jesus. What happened next left them wounded, exposed, and running—and forced an entire city to confront the difference between using Christ and belonging to Christ.
There is a sentence in the Bible that should make every person who casually says the name of Jesus stop for a moment.
Not because Jesus is weak.
Because His name is not a toy.
Not a charm.
Not a spiritual password.
Not a phrase you attach to whatever you already decided to do.
And certainly not a magic formula.
The scene is Ephesus.
A city where spiritual power, magic, religious practices, commerce, and superstition collided. Into that environment came the apostle Paul preaching Jesus Christ.
And something extraordinary was happening.
Acts 19 makes an important distinction before the frightening part of the story ever begins: it says that God was doing extraordinary miracles through Paul.
God was doing them.
Not Paul manipulating God.
Not Paul discovering a secret formula.
Not Paul learning the correct combination of sacred words.
God was acting.
That detail matters because what happens next is almost a photographic negative of it.
Some itinerant Jewish exorcists saw what was happening around Paul and apparently attempted to invoke the name associated with his ministry.
The Greek of Acts 19:13 says they attempted:
ὀνομάζειν ἐπὶ τοὺς ἔχοντας τὰ πνεύματα τὰ πονηρὰ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ
They tried to invoke “the name of the Lord Jesus” over those who had evil spirits.
Then came their formula:
Ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς τὸν Ἰησοῦν ὃν Παῦλος κηρύσσει.
In straightforward English:
“I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.”
Read that carefully.
Not simply Jesus.
The Jesus whom Paul proclaims.
There is something painfully revealing in those words.
Jesus was somebody else’s proclamation.
Somebody else’s Lord.
Somebody else’s relationship.
Somebody else’s testimony.
They had apparently seen enough power associated with His name to want its usefulness without necessarily bowing to His lordship.
And that is where an ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because you can grow up hearing your mother pray and still not know the Christ she prays to.
You can know worship songs.
You can repost Bible verses.
You can own three Bibles and leave all three unopened.
You can say, “God is good.”
You can wear a cross.
You can know Christian vocabulary so well that people assume you must be close to God.
You can even learn how Christians sound when they pray.
And still there is a question no religious performance can answer for you:
Do you actually belong to Jesus Christ?
Seven sons of a man named Sceva were doing what Luke describes.
Then something happened that they probably never expected.
The evil spirit answered.
The Greek wording of Acts 19:15 is chilling:
Τὸν Ἰησοῦν γινώσκω, καὶ τὸν Παῦλον ἐπίσταμαι· ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνες ἐστέ;
The sense is:
“Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize—but who are you?”
Imagine the silence after that question.
They entered expecting to command.
Instead, they were questioned.
They entered believing they possessed a formula.
Instead, their borrowed spirituality was exposed.
“Who are you?”
Then the man in whom the evil spirit was dwelling attacked them.
Luke says they were overpowered and fled from the house naked and wounded.
It is a shocking scene.
But if we turn Acts 19 into nothing more than a frightening demon story, we miss Luke’s point.
The hero of Acts 19 is not Paul.
The point is certainly not the demon.
The center of the passage is Jesus Christ and the incomparable authority of His name.
The sons of Sceva had confused the name with a technique.
Scripture will not allow us to make that mistake.
The authority of Jesus does not come from the arrangement of the letters J-E-S-U-S.
His name represents the Person.
The crucified Christ.
The risen Christ.
The reigning Christ.
The Son of God.
The Lord before whom every knee will ultimately bow.
There is no Christian incantation.
There is no collection of religious syllables by which human beings gain control over God.
Biblical faith is not learning how to manipulate divine power.
Biblical faith is surrendering yourself to the living Christ.
That difference exposes something uncomfortable.
Some people do not actually want Jesus.
They want what they believe Jesus can give them.
Peace without repentance.
Protection without obedience.
Blessing without surrender.
Heaven without holiness.
Forgiveness without admitting sin.
Resurrection without a cross.
A Savior who rescues them from consequences but never becomes Lord over their desires.
We can even turn prayer into a transaction.
“Jesus, fix this.”
“Jesus, give me this.”
“Jesus, remove this.”
“Jesus, open this door.”
And none of those requests are automatically wrong. Scripture invites believers to bring their needs to God.
But underneath all our requests sits a deeper question:
If Jesus gave you nothing else you wanted, would Jesus Himself still be enough?
That question hurts because it separates devotion from transaction.
Maybe you have been near Christianity for years.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong in faith.
Maybe you can discuss theology.
Maybe you serve.
Maybe you preach.
Maybe you sing.
Maybe you have learned to lift your hands while carefully keeping certain rooms of your heart locked.
Nobody sees them.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Secret messages.
Pride.
An affair nobody knows about.
An addiction hidden behind respectability.
Occult practices mixed quietly with Christianity.
Hatred you have renamed “discernment.”
Money controlling you.
A relationship you know is dragging you away from Christ.
A private version of yourself completely different from the person people see on Sunday.
Acts 19 asks a terrifyingly simple question:
Are you following Jesus...
or merely using His name?
And here is where this story becomes beautiful.
Because the story does not end with seven wounded men running through Ephesus.
It ends with a city being confronted by the holiness of Christ.
When people heard what happened, fear fell upon them, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
Then something happened that genuine encounters with God repeatedly produce.
People stopped hiding.
Believers came forward confessing and disclosing their practices.
Others who had practiced magic brought their books together.
These things had value.
Real financial value.
Luke gives the enormous combined figure of fifty thousand pieces of silver.
And they burned them.
Think about that fire.
Those scrolls represented money.
History.
Habits.
Former identities.
Spiritual bondage.
Things somebody could have sold.
Things somebody could have quietly stored away “just in case.”
But repentance does not ask, “How close can I remain to my old bondage without technically crossing the line?”
Repentance turns around.
They did not rename their darkness.
They did not put a Christian sticker on it.
They did not keep the scrolls beside their Scriptures.
They burned them.
Not because destroying objects purchases salvation.
It does not.
We are saved by the grace of God through faith, not by earning forgiveness through dramatic acts.
But when grace reaches a person, repentance becomes more than vocabulary.
Sometimes repentance has a sound.
A confession whispered through tears.
A deleted number.
A severed relationship.
A returned possession.
A browser history that will never be visited again.
An apology finally spoken.
A secret finally brought into the light.
And sometimes repentance smells like smoke because something you once treasured has finally lost its authority over you.
Maybe your “scroll” is not made of parchment.
Maybe it fits inside your phone.
Maybe it is a conversation.
Maybe it is an account.
Maybe it is an idol nobody else recognizes as an idol.
Maybe it is the secret thing you keep telling God you will surrender “eventually.”
You already know what it is.
And perhaps that is why this story feels uncomfortable.
Because grace does not merely comfort us while leaving our chains untouched.
Grace brings us to Jesus.
And Jesus loves us too deeply to make peace with what is destroying us.
But hear this carefully:
The Gospel is not, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
That would not be good news.
The Gospel is that sinners who could never rescue themselves have been offered mercy through Jesus Christ.
The same Jesus whose name cannot be reduced to a magic formula willingly went to the cross for sinners.
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Crucified.
He bore sin.
He died.
And He rose again.
Our confidence is not that we learned how to pronounce His name correctly.
Our confidence is Him.
His finished work.
His mercy.
His righteousness.
His resurrection.
His grace.
This is why Christianity is infinitely more than attaching “in Jesus’ name” to the end of a prayer.
Those words are precious when they express genuine dependence upon Christ.
But they are not magic words.
Praying in Jesus’ name is not slipping a divine password into the final sentence so heaven is forced to approve our request.
It means coming to the Father through Christ, dependent upon Christ, under Christ, seeking what accords with His character and will.
Jesus is not the stamp on our agenda.
Jesus becomes Lord of the agenda.
And there may be someone reading this who suddenly realizes:
“I know about Him...
but I do not know Him.”
Do not run from that realization.
That conviction can become the doorway to grace.
You do not need to pretend.
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic religious performance.
Come honestly.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Put your trust in Jesus Christ.
The One who exposes darkness is also the One whose blood cleanses sinners.
The One before whom demons tremble is also the One who welcomed broken people.
The King with all authority is the Savior who allowed nails to pierce His hands.
That is the scandal of grace.
The holy God does not pretend sin is harmless.
And yet the sinner who comes to Christ in repentant faith discovers mercy that could never be earned.
Maybe your story is scandalous.
Maybe people would look at your past differently if they knew everything.
Maybe you have spent years believing that what you did has permanently become who you are.
But the Gospel announces something stronger than your worst chapter.
Jesus Christ receives sinners.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
Jesus does not merely improve the ending of an old identity.
In Him there is new life.
That is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because the scandal never happened.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because your sin does not have greater authority than the grace of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
The sons of Sceva wanted the authority of His name without the reality behind it.
Ephesus learned differently.
The story moved from imitation...
to exposure...
to fear...
to confession...
to repentance...
to the magnifying of Jesus...
until Luke closes the scene by telling us that the word of the Lord continued to grow mightily and prevail.
That is the ending worth remembering.
Not demons prevailing.
Not magic prevailing.
Not human reputation prevailing.
The word of the Lord prevailed.
So perhaps the most important question is no longer what happened inside that house in Ephesus.
Perhaps the question is what happens inside you after reading about it.
What needs to come into the light?
What needs to be confessed?
What needs to be abandoned?
What have you been trying to control instead of surrendering?
Have you inherited somebody else’s Christianity?
Your parents’ Jesus?
Your pastor’s Jesus?
Your spouse’s Jesus?
Paul’s Jesus?
Or can you say from a surrendered heart:
Jesus Christ is my Lord.
Someone silently reading may need to discover that repentance is not the end of hope. In Christ, it can be the beginning of freedom.
And do not let this become another article you felt deeply for three minutes and then forgot.
Come back when temptation tells you Jesus can be added to your life without becoming Lord of it.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
Let truth travel farther than shame.
Supporting Gospel ministry is one practical way believers can help useful teaching reach others, but it should never be confused with earning God's favor or proving devotion to Him.
Do not borrow Jesus.
Do not merely quote Jesus.
Do not reduce Jesus to a formula.
Do not settle for knowing the Jesus somebody else preaches.
Come to Him.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow.
Because one day everything we used to hide will lose its hiding place, and on that day the only name that matters will not be the name we merely spoke—but the Christ to whom we belonged.
You were never meant merely to carry the name of Jesus on your lips; you were meant to lay your whole life at His feet.
